metric_rationale: This is a per-trial dissociation score exploiting both orthogonal dissociations in the design, rewritten as flat, dependency-free code (no imports, no nested functions, no try/except, no lambdas) to eliminate the transmission-level syntax failures of the previous two attempts. Construction: on each trial I compute (i) the TTB pick — the features are listed in descending-validity order (validities [0.95, 0.85, 0.75, 0.65, 0.5]), so the TTB cascade is just the lowest-index feature on which the two options differ — and (ii) the Tallying pick from strict feature-wise win counts. Trials where both theories agree (types 11-12, 16 trials/subject) are skipped. On full dissociation trials (types 1-6, 48 trials/subject), where TTB backs the option with FEWER cue wins and Tallying backs the majority-tally option, a choice matching TTB contributes +1 and one matching Tallying contributes -1. On tied-tally trials (types 7-10, 32 trials/subject), Tallying is structurally forced to exactly p=0.5 for every parameter value (softmax over tied scores is uniform and the lapse injects uniform), so any systematic choice is pure TTB signal: +0.5 toward TTB's pick, -0.5 away. Expected value under TTB-simulated data is 0.8*(2q-1) with q=(1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, which is strictly positive for any beta>0, eps<0.5; under Tallying-simulated data it is -0.6*avg(2p_margin-1), strictly negative for any beta>0. The mean gap is order 0.3-1.0 across plausible parameters while per-subject sd is only ~0.05-0.10 (80 informative trials pooled), giving a decisive Welch's t-test at N=25. The score is self-hedging: if TTB is simulated with weak beta, the tied-trial component still adds signal while dissociation trials shrink, and vice versa for weak Tallying parameters. The function is a simple mean of per-trial contributions, so it works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices, making the between-subject variance well defined.

The design factorially crosses the tally margin d (the ONLY input Tallying's prediction depends on) with the top-cue direction s (the ONLY input TTB's prediction depends on). I exploit both main effects simultaneously with a single OLS coefficient contrast: regress the chose-A indicator on [intercept, d, s] over all trials and return b_d - b_s. Under Tallying, p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*d) + eps/2, so the partial slope on d is strictly positive (up to ~0.125 per unit d when beta is large) while the partial slope on s is exactly 0 — s adds nothing once d is controlled. Under TTB, p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*s) + eps/2, so the partial slope on s is strictly positive (up to 0.5) while the partial slope on d is exactly 0 — within a fixed s-column TTB is flat in d by construction, and no (beta, eps) can change that. Hence the metric is positive under Tallying and negative under TTB, with a gap equal to the SUM of the two theories' signature effect sizes, making it robust: it discriminates even if one theory happens to be simulated with weak parameters, as long as the other shows its signature. Including s as a regressor also removes the mild d-s collinearity built into the 16 pairs (corr ~ 0.3), so the d-coefficient is a clean within-column slope rather than a confounded marginal. Per-subject computation is well-conditioned: every subject sees all 16 pair types x 6 reps (96 trials), d spans -4..+4 within each s-column, and the regressors are balanced (mean d = 0, eight s=+1 and eight s=-1 types). Per-subject sampling noise of b_d is small (~0.02) because it borrows strength across all nine d levels, and noise on b_s (~0.11 worst case, p=0.5) is dwarfed by TTB's s-effect (~0.5 at moderate beta). At N=25 the Welch t-test on the pooled point estimates with these between-subject variances yields a highly significant separation in every non-degenerate parameter regime.

CORE IDEA. The competitor (unweighted Tallying) has beta in [0.1, 20]; for the overwhelming majority of that range, softmax over the tallies is essentially deterministic, so its choice on any d != 0 trial follows the raw cue count with probability (1 - epsilon) + epsilon/2, i.e. ~0.87 on average over epsilon in [0, 0.5] (and > 0.75 even at epsilon = 0.5). My advocated theory is explicitly in the UNSATURATED regime (beta <= 0.55), and its validity weights compress the effective evidence far below the raw count margin: on the d = +1 trials the weighted margin m ranges from ~1.2 (A wins the three best experts) down to ~0.0 (A wins the three WORST experts, trials T10/T14), so p(follow the tally) is only sigmoid(2*beta*m) ~ 0.5-0.75, and even the d = 3 anchors only reach ~0.96 at the extreme corner. Averaged over the advocated parameter box, the predicted tally-following rate is ~0.63-0.66, versus ~0.86-0.88 for the competitor. So this single choice rate separates the two simulated theories by ~0.22 in mean.

WHY THE VARIANCE IS TIGHT ENOUGH AT N=25. The statistic is a simple binomial proportion over 54 decisive trials per subject (96 trials minus the 42 tied-tally trials). Per-subject SD is ~0.06 (binomial) plus ~0.07-0.08 of genuine parameter heterogeneity, giving between-subject variances of roughly 0.010 (self) and 0.008 (competitor). The standardized gap at N = 25 is t ~ 8 (p ~ 1e-9), far beyond the alpha = 0.01 threshold, leaving a large safety margin even if the simulator samples parameters differently than I assume (e.g., log-uniform beta for the competitor still yields t > 3; a fixed competitor draw of beta = 0.5, epsilon = 0 still yields t > 5).

WHY IT IS NOT TRIVIAL AND IS THEORY-RELEVANT. The metric directly engages the theories' central dispute about how evidence is scaled. Under the competitor, one cue win is one unit of evidence, so a 3-vs-2 count is a decisive, near-deterministic signal. Under validity weighting, winning three low-validity cues while losing the two best ones yields a weighted margin near zero (trials T10/T12/T14), so those choices are near coin flips - exactly the validity-weighting signature. The metric also operationalizes my theory's stated claim that humans sit in the graded, unsaturated softmax regime rather than the deterministic-tally corner: if humans were deterministic tallyers, this metric would approach ~0.9; the graded-evidence account predicts ~0.65. Note the tied trials (d = 0) are excluded because both theories are indifferent there, which removes the competitor's coin-flip noise and makes the per-subject estimate maximally stable. The metric is a plain choice rate, so it is identical whether computed on one subject's 96 trials or the pooled data (no grouping of unhashable list cells is needed), satisfying both evaluation levels.

This metric implements the HARD-CEILING knife (FACT 1) of the design on the trial family where the two theories are maximally separated in a parameter-robust way. On every trial with raw tally margin |d|=1 (trial types t1-t8: single top-cue discriminator, single low-cue discriminator, 4-low-vs-3-top sign-flip pair, 2-top-vs-1-low pair, and their mirrors; 48 of 96 trials per subject), the competitor's predicted agreement with the count-winner is (1-eps)*sigmoid(2*beta*m) with m = sum_j v_j^gamma * sign(a_j - b_j). Because gamma <= 0.7, beta <= 0.55, epsilon <= 0.08, and the mean of |m| across the 8 trial types is at most 1 (it equals 1 only in the gamma->0 limit and shrinks as gamma grows, since the low-validity discriminators lose weight), concavity of tanh bounds the competitor's expected value on this metric by 0.5 + tanh(0.55)/2 = 0.750 over its ENTIRE box — and at its self-described operating point (beta ~ 0.25-0.3, mild gamma) it sits near 0.55-0.62. Tallying, in contrast, predicts (1-eps)*sigmoid(2*beta) + eps/2 on every one of these trials: for any beta >= 1 (most of its [0.1, 20] range) this is >= 0.88*(1-eps) + eps/2, i.e. roughly 0.85-0.95 for moderate lapses. So the theories make almost disjoint predictions on this scalar, and the gap (~0.3 in typical parameterizations, >= 0.12 even in the competitor's most favorable corner gamma->0, beta=0.55) is large relative to per-subject noise: each subject contributes 48 Bernoulli trials, so the per-subject standard deviation is only ~0.05 (tallying-like data) to ~0.10 (competitor-like data), giving Welch t on the order of 10-20 at N=25. The metric is well-defined both on the pooled data and on each single subject's slice (every subject sees all 8 |d|=1 trial types 6 times), so the between-subject variance is a proper binomial-style variance rather than n/a. It is not trivially fixed under my own theory (its value depends on beta and epsilon, and would drop toward 0.5 if subjects did not tally), and on human data it directly adjudicates the theories' conflicting predictions: near-ceiling count-winner adherence on minimal-margin trials falsifies the bounded unsaturated-regime claim, while values pinned below 0.75 falsify high-beta tallying.

This metric isolates the single structural knife-edge between the two theories: the weight assigned to v=0.5 experts. The competing theory's weight w_j = max(llr_j - tau, 0)^delta is EXACTLY zero for v=0.5 (llr=0 <= tau) for every admissible (delta, tau, beta, epsilon), so on trials where all four diagnostic cues (v in {0.95, 0.85, 0.75, 0.65}) tie, it predicts p(A) = 0.5 exactly regardless of how many chance cues favor A or B. My advocated theory assigns v=0.5 cues weight 0.5^gamma in [0.62, 0.97], producing a graded preference for whichever side wins more chance cues. The metric selects exactly these 'chance-only' trials (8 of the 16 unique pairs: trials 1, 2, 3, 4, 11, 12, 13, 14 — 48 of 96 trials per subject), computes the signed chance-cue advantage k for A, and measures how often the subject's choice follows sign(k), mapped to [-1, 1] around the 0.5 chance baseline. Expected values: competitor -> 0 (pure binomial noise, per-subject variance ~4*0.25/48 = 0.021); my theory -> strongly positive (at representative parameters, p(A|k) = sigmoid(2*beta*0.5^gamma*k) gives accuracies ~0.59/0.68/0.76 for |k|=1/2/3, i.e., a metric around +0.3; even at the lowest beta in my box it stays above 0 for every subject since beta>0 and gamma<inf). The contrast is parameter-free on the competitor side (its entire box predicts exactly 0.5 on every chance-only trial) and sign-consistent across my entire parameter box, so the between-theory gap is large while per-subject variance is tight (48 binary trials per subject), giving a Welch t-test at N=25 a comfortable margin below alpha=0.01. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices, satisfying the acceptance-test requirements.

SSR = P(choose the high-validity side | that side faces >=2 opposing weak experts), computed over the five 'multi-weak conflict' cells K2, K3, M3, M4, R3 (40 trials/subject; mirrors make it side-bias-free). This is the cleanest behavioral readout of the super-expert exchange rate, which is the only thing the two theories disagree on (they share sign-vote architecture, softmax, lapse).

Why these cells: on them the choice margin is w_strong*k - w_weak*m with m>=2, so SSR is monotone in the strong:weak weight ratio. My theory's ratio w99/w_weak is at least ~1.6 across its whole box (log-odds compression with delta<=0.2 keeps a large super-premium; if weak validities are exactly 0.5 the weak weight is annihilated entirely, making the premium maximal), so it predicts SSR at or above ~0.50 (center ~0.52 with v_weak=0.51; ~0.74 with v_weak=0.50; up to ~0.81 at delta=0.2/tau high). The competitor's ratio v_hi^gamma/v_weak^gamma is at most ~1.6 and typically ~1.2-1.3, so 2+ weak experts always outvote one super expert: its SSR is strictly below 0.50 for EVERY parameter in its box (center ~0.38; range ~0.20-0.49; it only approaches 0.49 when beta~0 collapses all probabilities to chance, which still lies below my theory's typical values). The two predicted intervals are essentially disjoint, and the separation survives parameter heterogeneity: with per-subject parameters drawn from the boxes, my SSR mean is ~0.57 (sd ~0.13) vs competitor ~0.38 (sd ~0.11) under v_weak=0.51, and ~0.77 (sd ~0.07) vs ~0.38 under v_weak=0.50 — Welch t at N=25 is roughly 5.5-15 in all scenarios, far beyond the 0.01 threshold.

Why not other cells: single-weak conflicts (K1, R1) have small gaps (~0.05-0.07) and only dilute; weak-stack cells (W2/W3/W4a) have reversed but noisy gaps (8-24 trials, p far from 0/1) and would add variance faster than signal; G1 and the X1 tie are excluded because both theories (or side bias) contaminate them. Concentrating all 40 trials on the five cells with the largest, sign-consistent, box-robust gaps maximizes the mean difference per unit of between-subject variance, which is exactly what the Welch test rewards at N=25.

The single sharpest, most robust knife between the two theories in this design is the sign of the weight on the 99%-validity expert (feature 0). My advocated theory assigns w(0.99) ~ -1 trusted-cue unit (anti-diagnostic endorsement), while the competitor assigns it its largest positive weight (~1.16-1.36 cue units). Feature 0 discriminates on 9 of the 19 unique trial types (trials 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 15, 16, 17), i.e. 45 of the 95 trials per subject, so the metric averages over a large, pre-registered, sign-consistent family rather than a single cell.

Predicted values (center parameters, lapse included):
- Advocated theory: per-trial anti-follow rates ~0.87 (S1/S1m, trials 1-2), ~0.85-0.90 (trials 3-4, 7-8), ~0.93 (trial 15, the 0.90-vs-0.99 cell), ~0.96 (trial 17), ~0.42 (trial 16) -> pooled index ~0.84, with per-subject SD ~0.05-0.07 (45 Bernoulli trials plus modest parameter spread; the parameter boxes keep every S1-type anti-follow rate inside [0.79, 0.90]).
- Competing theory: anti-follow ~0.19-0.31 on the S1/D-type cells, ~0.40-0.52 on the near-tie cells -> pooled index ~0.33, per-subject SD ~0.07.

The mean gap (~0.5) is enormous relative to the between-subject spread, so Welch's t-test at N=25 separates the theories by many standard errors (t > 20 expected). The metric is a plain behavioral proportion (no free parameters, no fitting to either model), it is well defined both on the pooled DataFrame and on any single subject's slice (each subject sees all 19 trial types x 5 reps, so ~45 qualifying trials per subject), and it is robust to the exact validities of features 5-7 because it depends only on feature 0, whose validity (0.99) is fixed by the design. Under my theory the index is high (subjects are contrarians toward the near-certain expert); under the competitor it is low (subjects follow the near-certain expert). A value near 0.5 would be evidence against both.

The single sharpest, most parameter-robust dissociation in this design is the D-family: trials where the 98% expert and the 90% expert endorse opposite options while the 75% expert is tied (trials 15, 16, 19, 20; 4 reps each = 16 trials per subject). The metric is the per-subject (and pooled) probability of FOLLOWING the 98% expert's endorsement on exactly those trials. Under FDEI, delta in [0.1,0.2] compresses log-diagnosticities so heavily that w(0.98)/w(0.90) is at most ~1.12; the net evidence on a pure 98-vs-90 conflict is |s| <= ~0.14, and with beta <= 0.37 the predicted follow rate is boxed in [0.47, 0.53] for ANY parameter setting -- a coin flip. Under SITT, w(0.98) is negative (in [-1.14, -0.70]) while w(0.90) is at its trust peak (~0.95-1.06), so the net score against the 98% endorsement is large (|s| >= ~1.65), giving a follow rate <= ~0.08 even at the weakest parameter corner with maximal lapse. The two theories therefore predict ~0.50 vs ~0.06 on this scalar -- a gap of ~0.44 with tight binomial per-subject variance (<= 0.25/16 ~ 0.016 under FDEI, ~0.005 under SITT), so at N=25 the Welch t-test separates them by t ~ 14. The metric is also robust to whether the six weak experts are 0.50 or 0.55: FDEI annihilates 0.50 cues exactly and even with 0.55 cues the D-cell follow rate only rises to ~0.58, while SITT stays below ~0.10 either way, because the weak-cue contributions are small relative to the 98-vs-90 conflict. Unlike a whole-design fit or a crossover-ladder statistic, this single exchange-rate quantity is directly interpretable (it estimates the subjective 98:90 exchange rate) and is deliberately chosen to be insensitive to lapse rate, softmax gain, and weak-cue weighting -- the parameters the two theories share -- so it isolates exactly the structural claim (flat compression vs inverted-U trust with a cliff) on which they disagree.

I advocate BSST, whose signature is the sharp distrust cliff between v=0.98 and v=0.99 (w(0.99) ~ -1.1 trusted-cue units) plus a small negative weight on chance experts. The competing FDEI theory compresses diagnosticities so heavily (delta ~ 0.15) that a 0.98 and a 0.99 expert are nearly exchangeable (w99 - w98 in [-0.21, +0.15]) and chance cues are annihilated exactly. I therefore built the metric around the 10 pre-registered 'cliff conflict' trials (S1/S1m, S2/S2m, D1/D1m, D2/D2m, V1/V1m; 4 reps each = 40 trials per subject) in which exactly one option is endorsed by the 99% experts and the rival is endorsed only by <= 0.98-validity experts (the G1/G1m agreement anchors, where the 99-side also wins the 0.90 experts, are explicitly excluded by exact pattern matching). The metric is the rate of choosing AGAINST the 99%-endorsed option on these trials. Code-level recomputation of both predict functions over their full parameter boxes gives: BSST anti-99 rates of ~.86-.90 (S1), ~.90-.95 (S2), ~.72-.79 (D1), ~.85-.94 (D2), ~.70-.76 (V1) -> overall ~0.84; FDEI gives ~.42-.51 (S1), ~.30-.47 (S2), ~.47-.53 (D1), ~.44-.55 (D2), ~.27-.38 (V1) -> overall ~0.44. The contrast is sign-disjoint with a ~0.40 mean gap. Crucially the per-subject variance is small: each subject contributes 40 binary trials, so binomial sampling noise gives sd ~ 0.06 (BSST) / 0.08 (FDEI), and parameter heterogeneity within the boxes moves any single cell by at most a few points without ever flipping the favored side. Expected Welch t at N=25 is on the order of 15-20, far beyond the alpha=0.01 threshold, unlike small-effect contrasts (Z/X/P families, gaps ~0.03-0.10) which would be drowned in binomial noise at this sample size. The metric is a plain choice rate, so it is well defined both on the pooled DataFrame and on each single subject's 96-trial slice.

The single sharpest, most robust structural disagreement between FDEI and BSST in this design is the sign of the weight assigned to the 0.99-validity expert. FDEI's compressed-but-strictly-monotone weight function makes w(0.99) its LARGEST positive weight (about 1.16-1.36 cue units across its whole parameter box), so whenever the 0.99 expert discriminates, FDEI follows it above chance. BSST's distrust cliff makes w(0.99) strongly NEGATIVE (about -0.9 to -1.3 across its whole box), so BSST systematically chooses AGAINST the 0.99-endorsed option. In this 24-trial schedule, exactly 8 unique trials (trials 7, 8, 9, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21) have the feature-1 (0.99) expert discriminating; in every one of them the remaining discriminating cues form a balanced or weak background (mid-band cues split across sides, plus 0.5/0.55-flank cues that are near-zero under FDEI), so the 0.99 cue carries the sign of the evidence. With 4 repetitions this yields 32 informative trials per subject. Predicted values: FDEI ~0.62 (every parameter in its box gives follow-rates of roughly 0.56-0.73 on these trials, plus a small lapse pulling toward 0.5); BSST ~0.15-0.35 (anti-following on all 8 trial types under either the 0.5 or 0.55 flank-validity reading of the design, since the cliff weight dominates the balanced background). The gap (~0.3 in means) is large relative to per-subject sampling noise (binomial SD over 32 trials is about 0.08), so with N=25 subjects Welch's t-test separates the theories decisively. The metric is a plain behavioral proportion (no model fitting, no free parameters), works identically on the pooled data and on each single subject's slice, and is deliberately insensitive to the mid-band weight structure, the softmax gain, and the exact flank validities — it isolates exactly the one qualitative signature (follow vs. anti-follow a 99% expert) on which the two theories make opposite-signed, box-uniform predictions. It is not trivially true for FDEI: it is precisely the empirical claim at stake — that stated near-certainty is trusted (compressed, but not inverted) rather than distrusted — and a human follow-rate at or below 0.5 on these trials would falsify FDEI's entire parameter box.
